docs.title: Where to begin
docs.text:
The PlayStation 4 version of Bloodborne, running natively on Linux and the Steam Deck: the game's own code runs on the CPU and its graphics are translated to Vulkan. You need your own dump of the game with update 1.09; no game files are included.

Getting startedYour dump, the AppImage and the first launch. Playing onlineSeamless Hunt, The Hunter's Dream or your own server, and seamless co-op. Steam and the Steam DeckAdd to Steam, Game Mode, controllers and the Steam overlay. When something breaksCommon problems, and how to send a log.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• Online and co-op: messages, bloodstains, bells and summons, and seamless co-op that lasts through deaths, lamps and areas, with Linux and Windows players together.
  • Local co-op: 2 to 4 players on one PC, each with their own controller.
  • Hunter's Atlas: a fullscreen in-game map with fast travel to the lamps you have found.
  • Frame rate unlocked or capped at 30, 60 or 90, from 720p to 4K, and ultrawide screens.
  • FSR 3.1, FSR 4 and DLSS upscaling.
  • Any controller, with its own button prompts in the game, and keyboard and mouse.
  • Trophies, Discord status and Add to Steam in one click.
  • An AppImage for any distribution and the Steam Deck, which updates itself.

docs.title: Game compatibility
docs.text: bbport runs Bloodborne for PS4 with update 1.09. Its hooks and patches use the addresses of one executable: the launcher hashes the loaded eboot.bin image and runs only that one 1.09 executable (scripts/game_check.py). A dump that passes the check runs; one that does not is told why (no 1.09 update, another executable, or an eboot.bin with Lance McDonald's 60 fps patch baked in).

Checked means a dump of that release with update 1.09 had exactly the executable bbport runs. The others are accepted on the expectation that every release shares the same 1.09 executable; if one does not, the launcher says so instead of starting a game that would crash. A report of how yours goes is welcome either way.

The alpha tests (CUSA01318, CUSA01322, CUSA01333, CUSA01335) are not supported.

The Game of the Year and The Old Hunters editions include the DLC. With a base game (such as the US CUSA00900), dump your add-ons too: each one is a folder (SPEXPANSIONDLC03, SPDLCMESSENGER00…) with only sce_sys inside, because their data ships with the 1.09 update. Put them in one folder and choose it in the launcher (Setup → DLC folder), or set BB_DLC_DIR=/path/to/dlc for run.sh; the launcher shows how many it found. Each folder must keep the add-on's name (its entitlement label, such as SPEXPANSIONDLC03). Copying them to user/addcont/<title id>/, shadPS4's layout, works too.

docs.title: Tested with this fork
docs.text:
On Linux (CachyOS, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060), with the US release (CUSA00900):

  • The base game with update 1.09 and the add-ons dumped separately (The Old Hunters and the two messenger add-ons), from the launcher's DLC folder.
  • A dump whose eboot.bin had Lance McDonald's 60 fps patch baked in: the launcher reports it, and the clean 1.09 eboot.bin runs.
  • Every text and voice language the files have, through Game text language and Voice language: Spanish from Spain and Latin American Spanish among them.

The European Game of the Year edition (CUSA03173) is the release the original bbport is developed and tested with.

docs.title: Catching a crash with a debugger
docs.text:
By default a fatal fault or a GPU-library assertion ends the process at once: the log keeps one line (Host fault, Guest fault, STOP: GPU library assertion failed) and nothing else. BB_FAULT_WAIT=1 keeps the process alive at that point, stopped inside its handler, so a debugger can look at the faulting thread with its registers, stack and memory still there.

  1. Launcher → Advanced → Developer → Extra variables: BB_FAULT_WAIT=1 (or export it before run.sh). Nothing changes while the game runs; it costs nothing.
  2. When it crashes, the game freezes, a desktop notification says so, and the log ends with bbport: ... the process stays alive for a debugger: bash tools/debug_attach.sh <pid>.
  3. Run that line. gdb attaches, writes logs/crash-<time>-<pid>.txt and kills the process. With --keep it detaches instead, so gdb -p <pid> can be used by hand afterwards.

The report has every thread's stack, and for the faulting thread its registers, the instructions around pc and the top of its stack; for a GPU-library assertion the locals of the asserting thread (bt full). bbport's own frames carry file and line (the build is RelWithDebInfo); libc's come from debuginfod when it is reachable. Game code shows as a guest offset (pc minus the image base, as in the log's Guest fault line); the report gives an objdump command that disassembles out/boot-linked.bin around it.

GPU hangs are different: the device is lost and the GPU breadcrumbs in the log name the stuck draw or dispatch; the assertion that follows is caught the same way, but the state of interest is on the GPU.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text: The port reads a few hundred BB_* environment variables. Some are for players (upscaler, frame rate, controls); most are diagnostics and developer switches. The list below is every one the code reads, from the port's own registry (gpu/shim/bb_env_vars.def); tests/test_env_vars.py fails when the code and the registry disagree, so it stays complete. Everything from "Every BB_* variable" on is the output of python3 scripts/env_vars.py --doc (without its title); the sections above it are written by hand.

docs.title: How to set them
docs.text:
In the launcher: Advanced → Developer → Extra variables (NAME=value, space-separated). The settings key is extra_env in the launcher's settings.json, read by game_environment() in launcher/bbport_launcher.py:

  • The field is split on whitespace, and each piece at its first =: BB_UPSCALER=fsr4 BB_AUDIO_GAIN=1.5 RADV_DEBUG=nohiz.
  • There is no quoting. A value cannot contain spaces, and quotes stay part of the value. Use separators the variable itself accepts, such as ; or ,.
  • A piece without = is ignored. If a name appears twice, the last one wins.
  • Any name is accepted, third-party ones included (RADV_DEBUG, MANGOHUD, VK_*, __GL_*).
  • The result goes to run.sh. Both the launcher's Play button and --play (a Steam shortcut, the Steam Deck's Game Mode) use it.

From a terminal (source checkout): BB_GAME_DIR=/path/to/CUSA03173 BB_FPS=60 bash run.sh. Without the launcher, nothing sets the launcher's variables. run.sh then uses its own defaults (game folder ../CUSA03173, uncapped frame rate, and so on).

From a terminal (AppImage): BB_UPSCALER=fsr4 ./Bloodborne-bbport-x86_64.AppImage --play starts the game with the launcher's saved settings. Mind the precedence below: the launcher's own settings replace a variable of the same name from the shell. Extra variables replace both. The AppImage keeps its data (bbport.ini, saves, logs) in BB_DATA_DIR, by default ~/.local/share/bbport.

bbport.ini: many graphics options live in bbport.ini and the in-game menu, not in the environment. A few variables override those keys at start: BB_UPSCALER, BB_UPSCALE_PRESET, BB_FSR_SHARPNESS, BB_JITTER, BB_REACTIVE* and BB_OBJECT_MOTION (gpu/shim/bbport_settings.cpp). Values set this way stay in force until the next start.

docs.title: Precedence
docs.text:
The environment is built in this order; a later step wins:

  1. The environment the launcher (or the AppImage) was started with.
  2. The launcher's own settings (game_environment()): some are always written (the game folder, mods, languages, frame rate, fullscreen and the like) and replace a shell value; others only when the setting is on.
  3. The launcher's Extra variables.
  4. run.sh, which fills in what is still unset (the data folder, the online module, Discord).

Every BB_* variable the port reads, by kind, from gpu/shim/bb_env_vars.def (scripts/env_vars.py --doc). The game prints the variables set at its start (Environment: in the log) and warns about BB_* names it does not know.

=1: ... / =0: ... / =N: ... say what that value does; set: ... means any value turns it on (even 0).

docs.title: Layer memory module: PS4 GPU addresses without sparse (plan, 2026-10-09)
docs.text: Design notes from when this work was planned, kept for their reasoning. bbport 0.7 has one memory model and its own renderer, and some switches named here (BB_PC_MODEL) no longer exist; the current list is in ENVIRONMENT.md.

docs.title: Why
docs.text: The new memory model keeps game memory in a single sparse arena and moves blocks between game memory and VRAM by rebinding (vkQueueBindSparse). On NVIDIA (Linux, drivers ≥ 555), the bind time grows with the number of pages already bound, and the call holds a global lock: each move to VRAM cost seconds, and the game and the desktop froze (GTX 1660 Ti, 615.71). Without moves (BB_FIXED_ARENA=1) it runs at 48.6 FPS versus ~205 on an RX 7800 XT. We need a model that works the same on AMD, NVIDIA and Intel and is not tied to the shadPS4 buffer cache: part of a future layer for running PS4 games.

docs.title: Idea
docs.text:
The PS4 GPU has its own virtual memory (GPUVM) on top of shared memory; every V#, T# and pointer in user data is a virtual address. On PC we do the same with Vulkan 1.2 means (BDA):

  • Memory sources: ordinary (non-sparse) Vulkan buffers:
  • chunks of game memory: dma-buf (AMD) or host memory import (NVIDIA, Intel), one chunk per game direct memory allocation (allocations are mapped whole, so a range inside one mapping is always contiguous within one chunk);
  • VRAM mirrors: segments aligned to game addresses (game page X sits in the segment at the same offset), allocated when the first VRAM page appears in the segment.
  • Page table (a buffer on the GPU): page of a PS4 address → device address (BDA) of its current source. It is changed by a copy in the command stream, in order with draws, without semaphores.
  • Direct path: the whole V# range is in one source (almost all bindings) → an ordinary descriptor (source buffer, offset, size). The shader translator does not change.
  • Paged path: the range is mixed (≈85 huge bindings per frame: shaders bound to all of memory) → the descriptor points to a record {PS4 address, size}, and the shader translates each address through the table. A pipeline variant only for such bindings (specialization key).
  • Vertices, indices, indirect arguments, copies, texture uploads: the direct path; otherwise, assembly into a contiguous temporary buffer (read-only) or per-page copies (the CPU knows the table).
  • Moving to VRAM and back: the policy of the current new model (data whose writes we know about: loaders, the GPU; unknown writers stay in place), but the execution is a copy + a table write + choosing the source at bind time. Bindings recorded before a move read the old source, which is still valid; VRAM is freed once the GPU has passed those commands.

docs.title: Order of work
docs.text:
1. Module core (gpu/layer/, no dependencies on shadPS4): sources, pages, table, Resolve(address, size) → a direct source or "mixed", walking over sources for copies. The command recording interface is abstract (copy, table write), so it does not pull in the scheduler.
  2. Hook-up without VRAM: the new model returns ranges in place through chunk buffers, not through the arena; the new model does not create the sparse arena. Expected: ~48 FPS on AMD (like BB_FIXED_ARENA), no vkQueueBindSparse at all. Check the image, then make a build for NVIDIA.
  3. VRAM mirrors + moves: the policy from BufferCache, the page table, the paged path in shaders for mixed bindings. Goal: parity with the sparse arena on AMD (~205 FPS).
  4. NVIDIA/Intel: a test build, a tester log; then remove sparse from the new model entirely.

Measurements: RX 7800 XT, standing still (tools/bench.sh), BB_PC_MODEL=1; diagnostics BB_RESIDENCY_MIX=1.

docs.title: Status (2026-10-09, morning)
docs.text:
• Steps 1–3 are done. On the RX 7800 XT, standing still: module ~205 FPS, sparse arena ~205–238, old model ~220 (at the lamp in the Hunter's Nightmare); in another spot (1170 draw calls): 167.5 / 164.5 / 146. vkQueueBindSparse is never called in module mode (counter in the Layer memory: line).
  • Mixed bindings are solved without the paged path: "volatile" blocks (layer_volatile). A block with unknown bytes (the edge of a range, a gap between images) goes into the mirror together with the rest of the range, is refreshed from game memory before each binding, and whatever a dispatch wrote into it is copied back after the dispatch (LayerAfterBindings). The paged path remains for bindings of 64 MiB and larger. BB_LAYER_VOLATILE=0 turns it off (for comparison).
  • Default: AMD uses the sparse arena, other GPUs use the module (BB_LAYER_MEMORY=1/0 to choose manually). Step 4 (NVIDIA): needs a tester log; the host memory import path cannot be checked on AMD (RADV does not import memfd).

docs.title: Addendum: original copying and portable labels (2026-10-09)
docs.text: In the new module, the paged path of the original copy shader is fixed: writes update game memory and the current mirror; the native shader is now selected by default. For GPU labels, a standard Vulkan path without AMD buffer marker was added. The implementation, switches and verification limits are described in TRANSLATION_GPU_COPY_LABELS.ru.md. This removes the dependency of label writes on the AMD extension, but does not replace hardware testing on NVIDIA.

docs.title: Mods and third-party patches
docs.text: Both are in the launcher's Mods section and apply at the next start. The game folder itself is never changed.

docs.title: File mods
docs.text:
The Mods group has the folder, a Load mods switch, and the list of mods: each one can be turned on or off and moved up or down. The lowest mod that is on wins: when two mods replace the same file, the log says which one replaced the other.

The mods folder is ~/.local/share/bbport/mods/ with the AppImage (mods/ in the data directory when running from the repository). Extract each mod into a folder of its own:

mods/
  Mod name/
    dvdroot_ps4/
      chr/...
      param/...
      menu/...

These layouts work as well:

  • Mod name/app0/dvdroot_ps4/..., and Mod name/<title ID>/dvdroot_ps4/... with whichever release the mod was made for (CUSA03173, CUSA00900, ...).
  • Up to three extra wrapper folders, as extracting an archive into a folder of its name leaves it: Mod name/Mod name v1.2/dvdroot_ps4/... (notes, pictures and links may sit next to them: README, .txt, .pdf, .png, .webp, .url, ...).
  • The game's folders without dvdroot_ps4: Mod name/chr/..., Mod name/parts/... (chr, parts, map, menu, msg, param, sfx, sound, font and the other folders of dvdroot_ps4), also next to other folders such as Screenshots or Optional, which stay out of the game.

A folder in the mods folder that is not a mod is listed in the launcher under the mods with the reason: still an archive, several mods in one folder, no game files, or empty.

Upper or lower case does not matter: a mod made on Windows with DVDROOT_PS4/Chr/C0000.chrbnd.dcx replaces the game's dvdroot_ps4/chr/c0000.chrbnd.dcx. The log shows how many game files the mods replaced and added, e.g. Mods: 12 game files replaced, 0 added. A mod meant to replace files that says 0 game files replaced has its files in the wrong place.

What works: ready-made replacements of dvdroot_ps4 files (textures, models, params, interface, sound, fonts). What does not:

  • ZIP or 7z archives: extract them first.
  • Two mods changing different parts of the same .dcx or .bnd file: the last one replaces it whole, the files are not merged.
  • Mods that replace eboot.bin, sce_module or sce_sys, DLL injectors and script plugins. Changes to the game's code are patches (below).
  • Symbolic links inside a mod.

Whether a mod works with Bloodborne 1.09 is up to its author.

A shadPS4-style folder next to the game folder, <game folder>-mods/dvdroot_ps4/... (for example CUSA03173-mods next to CUSA03173), is loaded too, before the mods in the list. You can also choose a folder that holds dvdroot_ps4 directly as the mods folder: it is then loaded as one mod. Load mods turns all of them off. The field of view works the same way, as files laid under the mods; it is a setting of its own and stays on when mods are off.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
For each start, the data directory gets a merged tree of links, out/mod-game-*: the game sees the mods' files where they replace its own and the original files everywhere else. /app0 is read-only, and saves go to the usual folder. The tree is removed when the game exits normally or the launcher stops it; one left behind by a crash is not reused.

The order and the mods turned off are kept in mods.json in the data directory:

{"order": ["First", "Second"], "disabled": ["First"]}

New folders are turned on and added at the end, in alphabetical order.

From a terminal:

BB_GAME_DIR=/path/to/game BB_MODS_DIR=/path/to/mods bash run.sh
BB_GAME_DIR=/path/to/game BB_MODS_ENABLED=0 bash run.sh

BB_MODS_CONFIG sets another mods.json. BB_MOD_TRACE=1 (with BB_MODS_DIR) logs the first reads of files that come from mods, to see whether a mod is being used.

docs.title: Third-party patches
docs.text:
The Third-party patches group loads patches in the shadPS4/GoldHEN XML format from the patches folder: ~/.local/share/bbport/patches/ with the AppImage, or another folder chosen in the launcher.

  • Only patches for version 01.09 of eboot.bin are listed. Files for other games are skipped: a file applies when it lists any retail release of Bloodborne, or none.
  • Each patch starts on or off as the file says (isEnabled); the choice in the launcher is kept in patches.json in the data directory:
{"enabled": ["file.xml/Patch name"], "disabled": ["file.xml/Other patch"]}
  • Lines of type bytes, bytes16, bytes32, bytes64, float32, float64, utf8 and utf16 work. A patch with a mask line (a pattern search) or an address outside the executable is skipped whole, and the log says so.
  • They apply after bbport's own patches (patches/Bloodborne.xml), so where both change the same bytes, the third-party patch wins.
  • shadPS4's patch file can stay named Bloodborne.xml. In a file of that name, the patches named as one of bbport's own are left out (bbport's apply), and the rest start off until you turn them on, whatever the file says. An older package's copy of bbport's file adds nothing.
  • Patches that replace pointers in tables, such as 60 FPS++, are moved to where the game is loaded.

From a terminal: BB_PATCHES_DIR=/path BB_PATCHES_CONFIG=/path/patches.json bash run.sh.

This guide is based on bbport's MODS.md (Russian), by deadinside28.

docs.title: Online play and co-op
docs.text:
Online play is a beta. Messages, bloodstains and ghosts come from a community game server: Seamless Hunt's (the default) or The Hunter's Dream. Bells and summons go through a co-op pool, and then the players' games connect to each other. Linux and Windows players can play together: everyone needs the game at version 1.09 and the same pool.

shadPS4's public shadNet server no longer accepts bbport builds: it signs the game out right after the login ("The shadNet server doesn't accept this shadPS4 build" in the log), and the launcher says so. The pools for bbport are Seamless Hunt (the default), The Hunter's Dream's and a server of your own.

docs.title: Seamless Hunt
docs.text:
Seamless Hunt is a community server for Seamless Co-op (BBSC), where Windows players join with BBSC's package for the Windows port.

  1. In the launcher's Multiplayer → Online tab, turn on Play online and choose Seamless Hunt: its shadNet server, WebAPI and game server come with it.
  2. Type a name and a password under Account and press Create (once). The server wants an email for each account; the launcher makes one from the name, as Seamless Hunt's own tool does.
  3. Turn on BBSC in the Seamless co-op (BBSC) group and press Test in the Status row.

Its bloodstains and death visions crash the game with "Transaction failed", on Windows too: they are off by default, as in Seamless Hunt's package (Bloodstains on Seamless Hunt brings them back). Messages, ghosts and summon signs are not affected.

docs.title: The Hunter's Dream (with bbhost's players)
docs.text:
Choose The Hunter's Dream (with bbhost players) in the launcher's Multiplayer → Online tab. The game's online module talks to The Hunter's Dream itself, the way bbhost does (from bbport 0.7): nothing else runs next to the game. Its account is your Discord sign-in, the same one bbhost uses:

  1. Press Sign in with Discord. The launcher shows a code, copies it and opens The Hunter's Dream's page.
  2. On that page, press Sign in with Discord to link and sign in; back on the page, enter the code in the code field (not in Sign in with a code from the game).

No password is kept: the launcher keeps the sign-in's token with its settings. Sign out forgets it. Test checks The Hunter's Dream's game server and its co-op service. Seamless co-op (BBSC) is not available there.

Report problems here (issues), not to The Hunter's Dream's support.

docs.title: Your own server
docs.text:
Its owner creates the account (hosting your own server), or you make it with Create under Account when the server lets anyone register.

  1. In the launcher's Multiplayer → Online tab, turn on Play online, choose Your own server with its address, and enter the account name (not the email) and the password. The password is kept on this computer with the launcher's settings.
  2. Press Test in the Status row: the game server, the shadNet server, its UDP port and its WebAPI should all answer, and with the account filled in, the sign-in should work. A wrong name or password shows there (the server does not say which of the two).

If the game says you are not signed in to PlayStation Network, the shadNet login failed: the log then has a shadNet login error (code 8 is a wrong name or password). If the server did not answer when the game started, the game keeps trying in the background.

docs.title: Seamless co-op (BBSC)
docs.text:
BBSC (Bloodborne Seamless Co-op, by CLS_AMG) keeps a co-op session going through deaths, lamps, areas, bosses and the Hunter's Dream, for up to 5 hunters: the guest follows the host through lamps, sees the host's world (doors, bosses, lifts), keeps the items and echoes it gets, and enemies get stronger for every guest. It runs inside the game's online module (gpu/bbnet20/bbsc, BBSC 0.0.2 from bbport 0.7). It is new, and its own author marks much of it as untested.

  1. In the launcher's Multiplayer → Online tab, Turn on BBSC in the Seamless co-op (BBSC) group (on by default). While it is on, BBSC's bells replace the game's; turned off, the game's come back the next time the character is loaded (the save is copied to save-backups first). BBSC settings, folded under it, has BBSC's own options: what the guest shares with the host, five hunters, enemy scaling and its percentages per guest, shared progress and the rest; only the ones changed from BBSC's defaults are passed to the game.
  2. Every player of the session needs BBSC, the same version: on Linux this port, on Windows BBSC's package for the Windows port (its BBport release). A player without it plays the normal game.
  3. The server decides how much of it works:
  4. BBSC's game server (Seamless Hunt's, which comes with it, or your group's, hosted with it): everything, summons across areas and 5 hunters included. Set it as the Game server of the Online tab.
  5. The Hunter's Dream has no BBSC: the normal game's co-op, with bbhost's players.

With BBSC and BBSC's game server, two players who cannot reach each other directly (CGNAT, strict routers, two games on one PC) are connected through that server's UDP relay (port 3478); SHADPS4_P2P_RELAY=0 turns it off.

BBSC gives every character its own items, which cost no Insight: the Hunt Bell (call other players), the Kin Bell (join another player), the Bloodlust Bell (invade), the Duel Bell (PvP on and off during co-op) and the Parting Blank (end co-op). It takes the game's Beckoning Bell, Small Resonant Bell and Silencing Blank out of the inventory, and they do not come back when BBSC is turned off; BBSC's own items stay, with their names (scripts/bbsc_kit_texts.py), and work again when it is back on. Before changing anything it backs the saves up to user/bbsc/save-backups/: copy a character's save from there to play it without BBSC with its old bells. Its texts follow the language the game shows its text in (Game text language in the launcher, else the system's): Spanish, French, German, Italian, Portuguese and Russian; English otherwise. F8 puts you back on the ground if you get stuck inside another player.

Not yet tested with more than one player on Linux: one player alone works (its items, deaths, lamps, the Hunter's Dream). Report what you find with the log.

Its log is in user/bbsc/logs/ (in the AppImage, ~/.local/share/bbport/user/bbsc/logs/), and the game's log has its warnings (BBSC: lines). Not in the Linux build: BBSC's cinematic camera (L3 + R3 opens bbport's menu) and its own Discord status (bbport has one).

docs.title: Summoning in the game
docs.text:
• The host rings the Beckoning Bell (one Insight each time); the helper rings the Small Resonant Bell. With BBSC: the Hunt Bell and the Kin Bell, at no Insight cost.
  • Use the same password in the game's network settings, so you find each other whatever your levels.
  • Be in the same area, close to each other, with the area's boss still alive in the host's world.

docs.title: Ports
docs.text:
Co-op traffic is UDP, straight between the players' computers. With your own server on Tailscale (hosting your own server) it goes through Tailscale: turn UPnP off and skip this section. Otherwise each player has to be reachable from the Internet:

  1. The router. With UPnP on (the default), the game opens its port on the router itself: the log says P2P on UDP port <port>: asking the router to forward it (UPnP). A router without UPnP needs a port forward by hand (UDP, the port below, to your computer's LAN address).
  2. The port to open by hand or in a firewall is UDP 3658, the PS4's own, which the game uses by default (Co-op port (UDP) in the Online tab: 0 keeps it). The log says P2P transport on UDP port 3658.
  3. Open it in the firewall. UPnP opens the port on the router only, not in this computer's firewall. With ufw or firewalld on, the launcher's Multiplayer → Online tab says so and gives the commands. For ufw: 
    sudo ufw allow 3658/udp
sudo ufw allow from <router IP> proto udp    # the router's UPnP answers
    Windows players open the same UDP port in their own firewall.

A router whose public address is shared by many customers (CG-NAT) cannot forward ports: the log's UPNP: IGD found - external IP=... should be your real public address. Tailscale works behind CG-NAT too.

docs.title: Reading the log
docs.text:
Run with BB_GPU_LOG=info in the extra variables for the online details. In a summon:

Line Meaning signed in npid='...' The shadNet login worked. summon_messenger/create Your sign is placed (helper). summon_messenger/get, sceNpMatching2CreateJoinRoom, summon_messenger/request The host found the sign, made the room and sent the summon. signed out by the server The server refuses this build (shadPS4's public one): use Seamless Hunt, The Hunter's Dream or your own server.

docs.title: Hosting your own co-op server
docs.text:
Bells and summons go through a shadNet server. shadPS4's public one (srv.shadps4.net) no longer accepts bbport builds, and the public pools for bbport are Seamless Hunt (the default) and The Hunter's Dream's (the launcher's Multiplayer → Online tab; README). A group of friends can also run their own server: shadnet-p2p by Wozzardman, the shadNet server with that UDP port working and a summon service of its own.

With your own shadNet server, messages, bloodstains and ghosts come from the Game server field of the Online tab: The Hunter's Dream by default, or BBSC's game server (below). Windows players of Supermedo's port can join the same server.

Tested with two players, one on this Linux port and one on Supermedo's Windows port, over Tailscale, with the server below on a home server (Ubuntu 26.04): summons, a boss fight together and summoning again after the helper died.

docs.title: How it fits together
docs.text:
• One always-on computer runs the server: a VPS, a home server, or one of the players' PCs (then it has to be on while you play).
  • Everyone joins one Tailscale network (a tailnet): the server and every player. Tailscale gives each computer an address starting with 100. and encrypts the traffic between them. This matters: shadNet's login on TCP 31313 is not encrypted, so it should not be open to the Internet. And the games then reach each other over Tailscale too, so nobody has to open ports on their router.
Protocol Port Used for TCP 31313 Login and matchmaking UDP 31314 Each player's address, for the other player of a summon TCP 31315 WebAPI and the summon service

docs.title: 1. Tailscale
docs.text:
On the server and on every player's computer, install Tailscale (download; on Linux curl -fsSL https://tailscale.com/install.sh | sh) and sign in:

sudo tailscale up

The server's owner invites the players from the admin console (Users → Invite external users), and each player accepts the invitation and signs in on the computer they play on. Then, on the server:

tailscale ip -4    # the server's address, 100.x.y.z: the players need it
tailscale status   # every player's computer should be listed

docs.title: With Docker (any Linux)
docs.text:
This repository has a Docker image for it: tools/shadnet-server. It builds shadnet-p2p on Debian 13, because shadnet-p2p needs Qt 6.8 or newer and some distributions are older (Ubuntu 24.04 has Qt 6.4). It runs on any Linux with Docker, Ubuntu 24.04 included.

mkdir shadnet-server && cd shadnet-server
for f in Dockerfile entrypoint.sh; do
    curl -fsSLO "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ayozetr/bloodborne_linux/main/tools/shadnet-server/$f"
done
docker build -t bbport-shadnet .

Then start it, with the server's Tailscale address and a signup code of your own (letters, digits, - and _; the players never need it, only you, to create their accounts):

docker run -d --name shadnet --restart unless-stopped --network host \
    -v shadnet-data:/data \
    -e SHADNET_HOST=100.x.y.z \
    -e SHADNET_REGISTRATION_KEY=a-long-code-of-your-own \
    bbport-shadnet
docker logs shadnet

The log should end with the three listeners on the Tailscale address:

Unsecured TCP listener on: 100.x.y.z:31313. No encryption, use it only on trusted networks
STUN UDP listener on: 100.x.y.z:31314
WebApiServer listening on: 100.x.y.z:31315

SHADNET_HOST keeps the server off the computer's other networks. After a reboot, it waits until Tailscale is up. The configuration (shadnet.cfg) and the accounts (db/shadnet.db) live in the shadnet-data volume. To stop or update the server:

docker stop shadnet && docker rm shadnet    # the volume, with the accounts, stays
docker build -t bbport-shadnet .            # after downloading a newer Dockerfile

Then run the same docker run again.

docs.title: Without Docker
docs.text: Follow shadnet-p2p's README. It needs Qt 6.8 or newer: Arch Linux and its derivatives, Debian 13, Ubuntu 26.04, Fedora 41 or newer. On Debian and Ubuntu, install qt6-websockets-dev along with the packages it lists, or CMake does not find Qt's HTTP server module (checked on Debian 13 and Ubuntu 26.04). In build/shadnet.cfg, set Host to the server's Tailscale address (or 0.0.0.0), Matching2Enabled=true and RegistrationSecretKey to your signup code.

docs.title: A firewall on the server
docs.text:
With ufw, let the tailnet in:

sudo ufw allow in on tailscale0

docs.title: 3. Accounts
docs.text:
One account per player, created on the server with the signup code. The name is 3 to 16 letters, digits, - or _:

docker exec shadnet shadnet-sample 127.0.0.1 31313 register <name> <password> <email> <signup code>

127.0.0.1 works only when the server listens on every address (SHADNET_HOST unset or 0.0.0.0). With SHADNET_HOST set, use that address instead. The tool answers Account created successfully., or FAILED: Unauthorized when the code is wrong. Give each player their own name and password.

To back up the accounts, stop the server and copy the volume's db/shadnet.db.

docs.title: 4. Each player's launcher
docs.text:
In Multiplayer → Online:

Setting Value Play online On shadNet server Your own server Server address 100.x.y.z (the port, 31313, is added) WebAPI address Empty (the server's port 31315) Online ID / Password The player's own account UPnP Off (Tailscale needs no router ports)

Then press Test in the Status row. Every line should get a check mark, the shadNet server's UDP among them: it shows the address the server sees for you, a 100. one through Tailscale. An error mark on the UDP line means summons cannot connect: check that the server is running and that its log lists the UDP listener.

Summons go through the server's own summon service: the log of a game says Co-op: summon signs through http://100.x.y.z:31315.

Windows players set the same server, WebAPI and account in the Windows port's launcher.

docs.title: Seamless co-op (BBSC)
docs.text:
For BBSC with everything on (summons across areas, 5 hunters), the group also runs BBSC's game server next to shadNet. It is in this repository, scripts/bbsc_gameserver/bbsc_gameserver.py (Python 3, nothing to install), and it takes the place of The Hunter's Dream for messages, bloodstains and the server list.

  1. Turn on shadNet's seamless mode: run the shadNet container again with -e SHADNET_BLOODBORNE_SEAMLESS_COOP=1 (it is kept in its shadnet.cfg).
  2. Build and start the game server on the same computer, with the same Tailscale address:
mkdir bbsc-server && cd bbsc-server
for f in Dockerfile entrypoint.sh; do
    curl -fsSLO "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ayozetr/bloodborne_linux/main/tools/bbsc-server/$f"
done
docker build -t bbport-bbsc-server .
docker run -d --name bbsc-server --restart unless-stopped --network host \
    -v bbsc-data:/data -e BBSC_HOST=100.x.y.z bbport-bbsc-server
docker logs bbsc-server

BBSC_SHADNET is the shadNet server's address when it is on another computer. Messages, bloodstains and its logs live in the bbsc-data volume. Without Docker: python3 scripts/bbsc_gameserver/bbsc_gameserver.py --shadnet 100.x.y.z --host 100.x.y.z.

Port Protocol What 20443 TCP The game server (messages, bloodstains, ghosts) 20444 TCP BBSC's relay (warps, world sync, scaling) 18671 TCP Its bbhost-compatible service (BBSC_BBHOST=0, --no-bbhost, turns it off) 3478 UDP The relay BBSC players fall back to when they cannot reach each other directly

Each player then sets Game server to http://100.x.y.z:20443 in the launcher's Multiplayer → Online tab, keeps the same shadNet server and account, and turns on BBSC in the Seamless co-op (BBSC) group. BBSC finds its relay at the game server's address (or BBSC_RELAY, the relay address in BBSC's settings).

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• The log shows 127.0.0.1 or another address in the listeners: check SHADNET_HOST, or Host in the shadnet.cfg beside the server's executable.
  • Waiting for 100.x.y.z in the log: Tailscale is not up on the server, or the address is wrong (tailscale ip -4).
  • The game says it is not signed in to PlayStation Network: a wrong name or password (code 8 in the log), or two players using one account.
  • The test passes but summons fail: every player's computer must be in the tailnet, not only the server; tailscale ping <player> from each side. Everyone needs the game at version 1.09 and the same co-op mode.

See also Online play and co-op for the bells, passwords and log lines of a summon.

docs.title: Our own translator instead of shadPS4: structure and order of work (2026-10-10)
docs.text:
Design notes from when this work was planned, kept for their reasoning. bbport 0.7 has one memory model and its own renderer, and some switches named here (BB_CP_SHADOW and BB_CP_DECODER) no longer exist; the current list is in ENVIRONMENT.md.

Goal: move away from emulation and from shadPS4 code. We want our own PS4 command translator and our own graphics renderer that scale to other games (everything specific to one game lives in its profile, gpu/games/) and behave the same on AMD and NVIDIA. After that comes shadnet (online play).

docs.title: Current state
docs.text:
Borrowed from shadPS4 (gpu/VENDOR.txt, commit b4e7ae7 from 2026-09-24): about 116k lines.

Part Lines What it does Our work in it video_core/amdgpu 8.3k PM4 parsing (command processor liverpool.cpp), registers, tiling GPU-side labels, occlusion, predication, PM4 self-test video_core/renderer_vulkan 28.6k Vulkan renderer: pipelines, rasterizer, scheduler, presenter draw pipeline (stages A/B), recording threads, upscalers, background compilation video_core/buffer_cache 7.4k game memory for the GPU almost all rewritten (memory module, VRAM copies, traps) video_core/texture_cache 4.8k textures by address, detiling time-based collector, uploads shader_recompiler 38.6k GCN → IR → SPIR-V paged buffers (BDA), fixes core, common 21.8k VideoOut, GnmDriver, event queues, utilities vblank, labels

Our own code, outside shadPS4: gpu/layer/ (memory module BbLayer::GpuMemory), gpu/games/ (game profiles), gpu/shim/ (overlay, settings, hooks), the runtime in src/ (kernel, libc, files, saves).

docs.title: Target structure
docs.text:
Modules with narrow interfaces. None of them knows addresses in the game's code (that belongs to the profile), and none does the GPU's work on the CPU (that is emulation):

  1. memory: game memory in place, VRAM copies as a cache, shared tracking of page protection (write traps for copies and textures). Exists: layer/ + the module in buffer_cache_layer.cpp.
  2. cp: command processor. Parses PM4 into the translator's command stream (state, draws, dispatches, synchronization) in the order the GPU executes it. Replaces liverpool.cpp.
  3. state: context registers → pipeline keys and Vulkan dynamic state. Replaces liverpool_to_vk and the key building in vk_pipeline_cache.
  4. resources: V#/T#/S# descriptors → buffers, images, samplers (caches, detiling). Replaces buffer_cache, texture_cache (the buffer part is already almost ours).
  5. render: Vulkan. Command recording per thread, barriers, submission, presentation. Replaces renderer_vulkan (the scheduler and stages A/B are already ours).
  6. shaders: GCN → SPIR-V. The largest part; it is replaced last, stage by stage (decoder, IR, passes, code generation).
  7. platform: VideoOut, GnmDriver, kernel events (core/libraries), next to the runtime.
  8. games: game profiles (exists).

docs.title: Order
docs.text:
One module is replaced at a time. First an interface in our code with the shadPS4 code behind it as is, then our own implementation behind the same interface. After each step: the route (a route benchmark script (not in this repository), frames and snapshots), the PM4 self-test (BB_PM4_SELFTEST=1), unit tests, the game on AMD and (from tester logs) on NVIDIA.

Step What Why in this order 1 memory: shared tracking of page protection; write traps under textures by default; model 0.3 and the sparse arena are removed removes the rest of memory emulation and the dependency on game hooks 2 cp: the translator's command stream; MEM_SEMAPHORE, GPU time, compute queues done by the GPU the last emulation left is in the command processor 3 state + resources they build on 1 and 2; the buffer part is already ours 4 render the scheduler and stages are already ours; the rasterizer and pipelines remain 5 shaders the largest and riskiest; by then everything else is already ours 6 shadnet networking, once the graphics are our own

Steps 1 and 2 are the plan to move away from emulation (EMULATION_REMOVAL_PLAN.ru.md, section dated 2026-10-10).

docs.title: 2026-10-10: our own PM4 decoder (step 2, start)
docs.text:
• gpu/cp/: our own code, without shadPS4. Packet format and opcodes (cp_pm4.h), register file and decoder (cp_decoder.{h,cpp}). The decoder walks the buffer in stream order, applies register packets (SET_*_REG, CLEAR_STATE, registers written by draw packets), descends into nested buffers and hands each packet to a "sink" (BbCp::Sink) with the state already applied: draws and dispatches as typed calls, the rest as packets. The sink decides COND_EXEC. The decoder knows nothing about Vulkan, the game or where execution happens.
  • Unit test tests/test_cp_decoder.cpp (target cp-decoder-test): registers, partial writes, draws, dispatches, nested buffers, COND_EXEC, CLEAR_STATE, corrupt buffers.
  • Register addresses are checked against the shadPS4 layout at build time (static_assert). This found a bug: on CIK, CP_STRMOUT_CNTL is in uconfig (0xC03F), not in config.
  • Shadow check in the game (BB_CP_SHADOW=1): the new decoder parses every top-level buffer from the same state, and the register files are compared at the end of the buffer. On the route, all buffers matched (~800k buffers, ~200 million packets, 0 mismatches, 0 parse errors). Bloodborne does not use nested buffers (they are covered by the unit test).
  • Next: the decoder as a cursor (packet by packet, so the command processor loop can yield to other queues while waiting), the register file as shared state storage (its layout matches shadPS4 Regs word for word), then moving packet handling from liverpool.cpp into the translator's sink one packet type at a time, each time with the shadow check and the route.

docs.title: 2026-10-10: the new decoder is the real parsing path
docs.text:
• The decoder became a cursor (BbCp::Cursor: packet by packet, nested buffers at the caller's choice). The register file can live in the owner's storage (for the command processor, its regs, with the same word layout). A write observer (RegisterObserver, one call per packet) provides what draw preparation needs: the written blocks and the packet checksum.
  • ProcessGraphics takes packets and register writes from the cursor (BB_CP_DECODER=0 selects the old walk). What each packet does is still the old code. PM4 self-test: 11 of 11. The share of prepared draws is the same (747k used, 19k not, versus 755k/24k), so the checksums match. The image is the same.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: When asking for help, attach the log: in the launcher's Log section, Export log… saves it to a file and Copy puts it on the clipboard.

docs.title: The launcher rejects the game
docs.text:
The launcher checks the game folder before starting. What it says, and what to do:

Message What to do bbport needs the 1.09 update merged into the game folder Copy everything from the dumped 1.09 update into the game folder, replacing files (eboot.bin and sce_sys too). param.sfo is from 1.09 but eboot.bin is not Copy eboot.bin from the dumped 1.09 update over the old one. This eboot.bin has the 60 fps patch by Lance McDonald applied Use a clean eboot.bin from the 1.09 update. bbport has its own 60 FPS. This is not a retail release of Bloodborne Alpha tests and other games do not run. See supported releases. eboot.bin could not be read as a decrypted PS4 executable Dump the game and the update again. The game files are damaged The extraction tool broke compressed files (LibOrbisPkg PkgTool on .NET 6 or newer); the game would hang while loading. Extract the game and the update again with a fixed tool.

docs.title: The game shows New Game instead of my save
docs.text:
Saves live in the data directory, and each way of running the port has its own:

  • The AppImage: ~/.local/share/bbport/user/savedata/1/<title ID>/.
  • From the repository (run.sh): user/savedata/1/<title ID>/ in the repository.

To move a save, close the game, back up both folders, and copy the savedata folder over.

docs.title: DLSS is "not supported by this GPU"
docs.text:
The log says why, on a line DLSS: unavailable (...); the game then uses another upscaler.

  • DLSS needs a GeForce RTX (20 series or newer) and NVIDIA's own driver; it does not work with NVK (not an NVIDIA GPU, or this GPU or driver does not support DLSS).
  • NVIDIA NGX initialization failed: update the driver, and check that NVIDIA's CUDA/UVM module is loaded (sudo modprobe nvidia_uvm; the nvidia-modprobe package loads it when needed). With Secure Boot, a module signing key that is not enrolled stops it (Key was rejected by service).
  • DLSS Frame Generation needs a GeForce RTX 40 or newer; on older cards the log says so and DLSS itself still works.
  • From the repository, DLSS needs bash tools/build_dlss.sh once after build.sh.

docs.title: Spanish shows the Latin American text (or the other way round)
docs.text: The game picks a language's regional text by the dump's region and the system language. Choose the text you want in Setup → Game text language: Español for Spanish from Spain, Español (Latinoamérica) for Latin American Spanish. Voice language does the same for the voices.

docs.title: The game crashes after playing a while, on a card with little VRAM
docs.text: On a 6 GB card the texture cache can run out of video memory: the log then repeats Texture cache: memory pressure, ... (critical ...). Lower what uses VRAM: a 60 FPS limit, a lower output resolution, lower Model detail in the game's Display settings, and close other programs that use the GPU (browsers, video players, other games).

docs.title: The picture is stretched on an ultrawide screen
docs.text: Choose the screen's shape in Graphics → Display → Aspect ratio (Auto follows the output resolution): 4:3, 16:10, 16:9, 21:9 or 32:9. The view gets wider (or taller) instead of stretched, and the HUD keeps to the screen's edges; it changes live, in the game's Display menu too. Output resolution Auto is the monitor's own; any other size written as output_res=WxH in bbport.ini works too.

docs.title: Exit to desktop
docs.text: Exit to desktop is in the game's System menu and on the title screen, from bbport 0.7. The Quit to Desktop switch of earlier Linux versions is gone with it, and a third-party Exit Game patch is no longer needed.

docs.title: The port's menu opens by accident with L3 + R3
docs.text: From bbport 0.7, L3 + R3 opens the port's menu only when both are held for 0.8 seconds, so pressing them in a fight (lock-on and camera reset) no longer opens it. Controls → Port menu from the controller can make it 2 seconds, or turn it off so that only Insert on the keyboard opens the menu. Closing it with L3 + R3 always works.

docs.title: The controller does nothing when the game is started from Steam
docs.text: With Steam Input on, Steam hides the controller and the game gets Steam's virtual one, whose input Steam sends only to the window it sees focused. On a Wayland desktop Steam sees only X11 windows, so the game now opens its window through Xwayland when Steam made a virtual controller for it (the log says Window: X11 (Xwayland), so Steam Input reaches the game). On older releases, put SDL_VIDEO_DRIVER=x11 %command% --play in the shortcut's launch options (keep --play after %command%), or turn Steam Input off for the shortcut: the game reads the controller itself.

docs.title: The Steam overlay does not open in the game
docs.text: Steam's overlay (Shift+Tab, its FPS counter, F12 screenshots) needs the game started from Steam, with Steam overlay on under Add to Steam in the launcher (on by default). The log then says Steam overlay: …/ubuntu12_64/gameoverlayrenderer.so. Without that line, the game was not started by Steam.

docs.title: The camera turns much faster on diagonals
docs.text: With the right stick pushed all the way, the game switches to its fast turn (about twice the speed), and it does so on diagonals too, not only straight sideways. That is how the game turns on a PS4 as well, with any controller. Controls → Even camera speed on diagonals keeps diagonals at the normal speed; the fast turn stays when the stick is pushed straight sideways. With it on the camera can feel heavier: the game's own Camera speed setting makes up for it.

docs.title: Summons never connect
docs.text: Press Test in the Status row of Multiplayer → Online. An error mark on the shadNet server's UDP line means the server never learns your address, and no summon can connect: check that the server is running and that its log lists the UDP listener, and that no firewall blocks UDP 31314 on its side (hosting your own server). shadPS4's public server does not accept bbport builds at all: use The Hunter's Dream, Seamless Hunt or your own server.

docs.title: Other online problems
docs.text: See Online play and co-op: the account, the bells, the ports and the log lines of a summon.

docs.title: Is this an emulator?
docs.text: No. The game's own code runs directly on the CPU, and its graphics are translated to Vulkan. It is built on bbport by deadinside28.

docs.title: Where do I get the game?
docs.text: From your own PS4: a dump of your copy with update 1.09. No game files are included, and none can be shared here.

docs.title: Can I play with Windows players?
docs.text: Yes. On Seamless Hunt or The Hunter's Dream, Linux and Windows players play together; for seamless co-op everyone needs the same BBSC version (0.0.2). Online play.

docs.title: Summons take a long time
docs.text: Some waiting is normal: the game checks for summon signs about every 35 seconds, as the PS4's servers had it, so a sign can take over half a minute to show up.

docs.title: My friend never gets summoned with the Kin Bell
docs.text:
It depends on the server:

  • On Seamless Hunt (or your own server with BBSC's game server), seamless co-op works fully: summons across areas and up to 5 hunters.
  • On The Hunter's Dream there is no seamless co-op: summons are the normal game's, with the Beckoning Bell and the Small Resonant Bell. Both hunters must be in the same area, the area's boss must still be alive in the host's world, and your levels must be within range (or use the same password).

Seamless co-op on each server.

docs.title: Do I need to open ports on my router?
docs.text: Usually not: with UPnP on (the default) the game opens its port on the router by itself, and with seamless co-op (BBSC) on Seamless Hunt relays players who cannot reach each other directly. A router without UPnP, or a firewall on your computer, needs UDP 3658 opened (ports). With your own server, Tailscale takes care of it.

docs.title: How do I use the in-game map?
docs.text: In the launcher, Mods → Map (Hunter's Atlas): turn on In-game map and press Prepare once. It makes the maps from your own game files (it downloads about 200 MB of tools the first time). In the game, choose Map in the quick menu (its fourth tile), press M, or with a controller open the game's menu and click the right stick (R3). The port's menu (Insert, or hold L3 + R3) changes the key and the controller shortcut. Travel to lamps from the map and Items on the map are in the same launcher group.

docs.title: How do I get FSR 4.1.2 (INT8, for RDNA2 and the Steam Deck)?
docs.text: FSR 4.1.2's models are built from AMD's own files, which can't be shipped here. In Graphics → Upscaler, on FSR 4.1.2 from AMD's driver, press Choose a file… and pick AMD's Adrenalin 26.10.1 or newer installer (the .exe) or the amdxcffx64.dll inside it. It also needs AMD's FSR 4.1.x upscaler DLL (amd_fidelityfx_upscaler_dx12.dll, from OptiScaler or a game with FSR 4.1): if you built FSR 4.1.1 before, it uses that one, otherwise it asks for it. It takes about 4 minutes. In the game, the port's menu chooses the model (INT8 RDNA2 or INT8 Lite).

docs.title: How do I get a log on the Steam Deck?
docs.text: Turn on Advanced → Developer → Save the log and statistics to a file once in Desktop Mode; Game Mode sessions then save theirs too. Getting a log.

docs.title: The game updated and my Steam shortcut stopped working
docs.text: Press Add to Steam again in the launcher: it updates the shortcut.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Your own dump of Bloodborne with update 1.09, from your PS4: any retail release (US, Europe, UK, Japan, Asia, and the editions with The Old Hunters). No game files are included, and other versions of the game's executable start and then crash. Which releases work.
  • Linux x86-64 and a GPU with Vulkan 1.3: AMD or Intel with Mesa, or NVIDIA with NVIDIA's driver. The Steam Deck works too.
  • About 6 GB of free memory, 10 GB for 1440p or 4K.

docs.title: First launch
docs.text:
1. Download Bloodborne-bbport-x86_64.AppImage from the latest release.
  2. Make it executable (in a file manager: Properties → Permissions → Allow executing, or chmod +x Bloodborne-bbport-x86_64.AppImage) and run it.
  3. In the launcher, choose your game folder: the one with eboot.bin in it.
  4. Press Play.

The first minutes

The first time, the game builds its shaders as it meets them, so it can stutter for a few minutes. The next sessions start with them ready.

docs.title: Saves, settings and the DLC
docs.text:
• Saves and settings go to ~/.local/share/bbport.
  • Setup → Saves exports your saves into a .zip and imports them back, also from shadPS4.
  • The Game of the Year edition already has The Old Hunters. With the base game, put its DLC folder in Setup → DLC folder.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text: The launcher's About page says when a new release is out and installs it; it can also go back to an earlier one. Your saves and settings stay as they are.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Play online, alone or in seamless co-op.
  • Add the game to Steam, or play on the Steam Deck.
  • Something wrong? Troubleshooting and getting a log.

docs.title: Getting a log
docs.text: A log is the first thing needed to fix a problem: it says what the game and the GPU were doing.

docs.title: From the launcher
docs.text:
1. Turn on Advanced → Developer → Save the log and statistics to a file. It stays on.
  2. Play until the problem happens, then close the game.
  3. The log is in ~/.local/share/bbport/logs, named after the time the game started (20261026_183438.log). The launcher's Log page shows the last one too.

This also works when the game is started from Steam or from the Steam Deck's Game Mode: turn the option on once in the launcher, and every session saves its log.

The log's first line says which version ran, and for a test build which one (bbport Linux 0.70-linux.1, build 74b1a308 HEAD 2026-11-03 (bbport 0.7)).

docs.title: Sending it
docs.text:
Open an issue and attach the .log file. It helps a lot to say:

  • what happened, and roughly when (an area, a boss, a menu, after a lamp travel);
  • your distribution, GPU and driver;
  • the upscaler, preset and output resolution;
  • for online problems, which server and whether seamless co-op (BBSC) was on, and the other player's log too if you can.

Crashes

Advanced → Developer → Crash diagnostics adds checks that point at what went wrong in some crashes. The game runs a bit slower with it on: turn it on when asked in an issue.

docs.title: Parallel GPU command processing — design notes
docs.text:
Design notes from when this work was planned, kept for their reasoning. bbport 0.7 has one memory model and its own renderer, and some switches named here (BB_UFFD) no longer exist; the current list is in ENVIRONMENT.md.

Goal: remove the single-core bottleneck of the emulated GPU command processor (shadPS4:GpuCommandProcessor, ~100% of one core while the rest of the CPU idles).

docs.title: Measurements (Bloodborne, Hunter's Nightmare, ~70 FPS, BB_DCB_STATS=1)
docs.text:
Graphics command buffers submitted 4200–5800/s, ~65–80 per frame Draws ~110 000/s, ~1600 per frame Draws per command buffer mostly 10–99, max ~200 Nested IndirectBuffer none State before the first draw ~118 context + ~31 SH register dwords written; only 8% start with ClearState

GPU thread profile after the single-thread work (perf, cpu-clock:u): texture binding ~25%, pipeline selection ~19% (StageSpecialization build/compare, sharp fetches), buffer binding ~14%, render targets ~8%, PM4 decode ~3%.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Command buffers are not self-contained: register state is inherited, so a worker needs the register state at the start of its buffer (context + SH ranges are ~6–8 KiB; one snapshot per buffer is ~40 MB/s at 70 FPS).
  • Draw preparation reads guest memory, not only registers: extended user data (EUD) and shader code. Earlier packets in the stream (DMA, WriteData, constant-engine dumps) can change that memory, so work done ahead of the GPU thread may see stale data.
  • The caches (buffer, texture, pipeline) and per-draw scratch state (flags in Image, user data inside shared Shader::Info) are single-threaded by design.
  • Image layout and barrier tracking assume one ordered stream.

docs.title: Plan
docs.text:
1. Speculative draw preparation on workers, validated on the GPU thread. A cheap serial pass records the register state at the start of each command buffer. Workers replay their buffer's register writes and, per draw, precompute the pure parts: pipeline key and stage specialization inputs, sharp fetches, texture and render-target descriptions, dynamic state values, vertex buffer ranges. Each result carries the flattened user data it was computed from. The GPU thread still decodes the stream and refreshes the flattened user data (cheap), compares it with the worker's copy, and uses the prepared draw only on a match; otherwise it computes as today. Correctness never depends on the workers. Prerequisite refactor: sharp consumers read user data through a view instead of the shared Shader::Info members, and per-draw scratch moves into a context struct.
  2. Thread-safe cache lookups. Finding existing buffers/images/views moves to the workers; creation, uploads, barriers stay on the GPU thread.
  3. Parallel Vulkan recording. Each worker records its own command buffer; they are executed in submission order with barriers at the seams.

Every step keeps a BB_TOGGLE_FILE bit so it can be switched off at run time and compared by screenshot and frame rate.

docs.title: Portability
docs.text: Must scale down to the Steam Deck (4 cores / 8 threads): worker count follows hardware_concurrency(), no busy waiting when cores are scarce, no AVX-512.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Step 1 (draw preparation, 4 workers, toggle 8192), Hunter's Nightmare, same view: 71.5 FPS with prepared draws vs 64.1 without (+11.5%), identical screenshots. 97–98% of direct draws use the prepared pipeline; each bb:DrawPrep worker ~10% of a core. The GPU thread is still ~90% busy: texture/buffer binding is the next target (step 2).

Guest write faults (same view, toggle 65536): the game fills its per-frame buffers sequentially and each 4 KiB page cost a protection fault — ~115k faults/s, ~20% of every GXWorker and of the main thread spent in the kernel. Unprotecting the aligned 64 KiB window around a fault: 16k faults/s, kernel time ~8%, 81.0 FPS vs 66.4 (+22%), identical frames. The GPU command thread is back at ~100%: it is the limit again.

Rejected: "hot pages" (never re-protect pages written repeatedly, upload them on every binding) — the set grew to ~14k pages, re-uploads dropped the frame rate to 33 FPS and a GPU ring timeout followed. Left opt-in behind BB_HOT_PAGES=1.

Texture description cache 2-way/4096, same-target fast path, LRU touch skip, no per-texture meta lookup: other outdoor view, 93.9 FPS; with the texture memos off (mask 1056) 65.6 FPS. Close to the 100 Hz display cap (vblank-paced), so further gains need an uncapped test.

docs.title: Streaming stutter (BB_FRAME_STATS "Stall:" lines)
docs.text:
Running through new areas gave 60–170 ms frames (also in shadPS4). The GPU thread was busy the whole frame, mostly in the kernel, uploading 50–400 MB of textures and buffers per frame. Findings, in the order they were fixed:

  1. Guest-to-staging copies ran on one thread (the recording thread, textures on the GPU thread). They now start at once on copy threads (BbCopy::Async, bbport_copy.cpp); small copies are batched per thread (one wakeup per ~512 KiB — one per copy cost 25% FPS). Guest-visible fences and queue submission wait for them (Scheduler::WaitHostCopies), which keeps the fix for UI flicker (the guest reused buffers before deferred copies ran).
  2. Copies then ran at 0.2–0.4 GB/s per thread, almost all in the kernel: the first CPU access to a new staging block makes the kernel allocate and clear it (~2 ms per 16 MiB), and the staging pool freed blocks after 3 s idle, between streaming bursts. It now keeps 512 MiB (BB_STAGING_KEEP_MB), frees the rest after 30 s and populates 128 MiB at startup.
  3. Write faults: a 256 KiB unprotect window (BB_FAULT_WINDOW) halves them again. BB_UFFD=1 tracks writes with userfaultfd write-protection instead of mprotect (no address-space write lock, no mapping splits); read protection for readbacks still uses mprotect. It removes the mprotect time but did not change the stalls measurably; opt-in.
  4. File reads into write-protected guest pages failed with EFAULT (kernel copies do not reach the fault handler); reads now touch each destination page first.

Result: stalls are mostly 40–50 ms (GPU thread ~30 ms of draw work plus ~12 ms of copies) instead of 60–170 ms; the area load frame 350 ms instead of 430–760 ms.

docs.title: Step 2, first slice: resource sharps on the workers (2026-09-30)
docs.text:
A prepared stage now also carries the sharps its worker read from the flattened user data: every T# with its texture-description hash, every S# and V# (PrepareResources, PreparedStage::image_sharps and siblings, in the arena of the submission). The GPU thread uses them when PipelineCache::UsedPrepared() reports that the draw's pipeline came from the prepared draw — the flattened data was then compared word for word, and sharps depend on nothing else. Resource list sizes are checked per stage. Toggle 4096 switches it off.

A/B in one run, standing still, BB_FPS_LIMIT=0, FSR 4, 20 s phases: 69–70 FPS with the prepared sharps, 66.5–67 without (+3%), same image.

Upscaler costs removed from the GPU thread before this (perf, DWARF call graphs): per-draw driver format queries in SceneTargets::Eligible (~13%), direct recording forced by CommandBuffer() in object motion and the reactive mask, index-list scans for object motion (~10%, now Motion::IndexRangeCache).

What remains on the GPU thread is mostly work on shared cache state: texture binding ~23% (FindView ~5.6%, UpdateImage/Track/Touch ~5%, barriers), buffer binding ~12% (ObtainBuffer ~11%), render targets ~8%. The next step is a draw-level split: the GPU thread keeps decode, cache mutation and barriers; a second ordered stage builds descriptor writes and vertex input state from the resolved handles.

docs.title: Scaling to the available threads (2026-09-30)
docs.text:
Draw preparation used to replay the whole command stream in every worker and was switched off below 12 hardware threads (Steam Deck: no workers). Now:

  • One scanner (bb:DrawScan) replays the register writes in order and stores, per buffer, its starting checksum and a delta of the 32-word register blocks it wrote (AmdGpu::RegDirty/RegDelta, recorded by ApplyGraphicsRegisterPacket).
  • Workers (bb:DrawPrepN, half the hardware threads in the affinity mask, 1..8) claim the nearest scanned buffer ahead of the GPU thread, reach its starting state by applying the deltas since their last buffer (or from the queue's tail state), and prepare its draws. More workers now mean more buffers prepared in parallel, not more duplicated replay.
  • All helpers are SCHED_IDLE (bbport_threads.h): they only take idle cores. If the scanner starves (busy CPU), the GPU thread rebases it from its own register state once the lag passes 64 buffers instead of queueing without bound (scanner rebases in the stats).
  • Copy threads use the same affinity count (critical path, normal priority).

A/B in one run (toggle 8192, standing still, BB_FPS_LIMIT=0, FSR 4), ~98% of direct draws prepared, no rebases:

CPU with preparation without 16 threads, 8 workers ~74 FPS ~57.7 FPS taskset -c 0-3,8-11 (4 cores / 8 threads, Deck-like), 4 workers ~68 FPS ~53 FPS

The previous design (4 replaying workers) gave ~69 FPS at the same spot on 16 threads, and none on 8.

docs.title: Vertex inputs on the workers (2026-09-30)
docs.text:
PreparedDraw::vertex holds, for the dynamic vertex input path, the attribute and binding descriptions (GetVertexInputs), the V# of every stream, the stream memory merged into ranges with each stream's range index, and the XXH3 of the streams (object motion). The GPU thread only obtains the buffers of the merged ranges and records the bindings. Used when the prepared draw's pipeline was taken, the attribute count matches the pipeline's fetch shader and no frame capture runs; toggle 4096 switches it off together with the sharps.

A/B (standing still, BB_FPS_LIMIT=0, FSR 4, 16 threads): ~69.3 FPS on, ~65.7 off (+5.5%; the sharps alone gave +3%). Screenshots identical.

Render targets were looked at and left on the GPU thread: their descriptions are already memoized per slot (key copy + compare), the size hint (last_cb_extent) is GPU-thread state rather than register state, and the rest of BeginRendering is view lookup, barriers and the reduced-resolution proxies — all on shared mutable state.

docs.title: Engine short paths: investigation (2026-09-30, in progress)
docs.text:
• The eboot has no symbols but links Sony's Gnmx (sdk\target\src\gnmx\gfxcontext.cpp, lwgfxcontext.cpp); FromSoftware's Dantelion2 CoreGraphics2 sits on top; YEBIS does the post-processing.
  • BB_BUFFER_STATS=1 (buffer_cache.cpp) prints buffer bindings per guest region every 5 s. Almost all traffic comes from the engine's frame ring, ~0x1043400000–0x1049xxxxxx inside the 2.4 GB direct allocation at 0x1042c00000: ~400k small constant copies/s (~190 MB/s) and ~850 MB/s of arena re-uploads after CPU writes (~13 MB per frame).
  • Candidate short path: import that ring into Vulkan (VK_EXT_external_memory_host) so the GPU reads it in place — no copies, no page tracking, far fewer GPU-thread operations. Blocker to resolve first: EOP fences are signalled when the GPU thread records the packet, not when the GPU executes it, so the guest may rewrite ring data still unread by the GPU. With ~100 MB of ring and ~13 MB per frame the wrap is ~7–8 frames; the GPU's lag is bounded by the presenter's frame pool (present_frames, swapchain image count). Next: measure the ring's wrap period per frame and the real GPU lag, then prototype the import behind a toggle.

docs.title: Measurements for the frame-data window (BB_BUFFER_STATS=1)
docs.text:
• Reuse distance of 64 KiB blocks in 0x104xxxxxxx: overwhelmingly 1 frame (then 2). The engine rewrites the same memory every frame; there is no long ring.
  • GPU lag when the GPU thread starts a frame (GPU lag at frame start): almost always 0 — the GPU has finished the previous frame. But the engine writes the next frame's data while the GPU still executes the current one, and EOP fences are signalled at record time. Reading this memory in place (VK_EXT_external_memory_host) is therefore unsafe unless fences wait for real GPU completion, which costs the guest (it waits on them). Dropped.
  • Per second in the hot window: ~370k small constant copies (~179 MB, ~480 B each) and ~3.6k arena bindings covering ~13.8 GB (≈3.8 MB per binding) of which only ~516 MB are re-uploaded. Copying bound ranges instead of tracking pages would multiply the traffic by ~27 (why the "hot pages" attempt fell to 33 FPS); page tracking is the right mechanism there.
  • Remaining candidates: per-submission snapshots of the constant area (fewer, larger copies instead of ~6000 per frame) and trimming vertex-buffer bindings to the index range a draw uses (the V#s cover whole vertex pools, so each binding walks ~950 tracked pages).

docs.title: Tried and reverted: per-epoch constant chunks
docs.text:
Small read-only constants served from one snapshot per chunk and queue-task epoch (the epoch changed at every task entry and resume, so a chunk only served data written before its copy). A/B in one run, standing still: 32 KiB chunks 82/82/79 FPS vs 85/84/84 without (slower: the extra copied bytes cost more than the saved operations); 8 KiB chunks 85/85/85 vs 85/83/85 (no difference). The per-binding constant copies are not what limits the frame; the change was removed. BB_BUFFER_STATS=1 (bindings per region, reuse distance, GPU lag) stays.

State after this work, standing still, BB_FPS_LIMIT=0, FSR 4: 82–85 FPS; GPU command thread ~90% of a core, recording thread ~92% (mostly its spin), GPU ~70% busy.

docs.title: Texture binding: repeated sets and the UpdateImage fast path
docs.text:
• Measured and dropped: only ~13% of draws bind exactly the textures and samplers of the previous draw in every stage (running through Yharnam), so skipping whole texture sets would save at most ~3% of the GPU thread.
  • TextureCache::UpdateImage runs for every texture binding; for a clean, registered image already tracked and touched in this GC period it only took the texture-cache mutex (shared with the guest threads' fault handlers). It now returns without the lock in that case, reading the flags atomically (toggle 1073741824 = 1 << 30 restores the locked path). A/B, 8 phases of 20 s: 81.8 vs 80.2 FPS mean (+2%), 3 of 4 pairs ahead; the game window was partly covered by other applications during the run, so treat it as indicative.
  • The A/B script now records the log line at each phase switch and prints per-phase means.

docs.title: LTO and PGO (2026-09-30)
docs.text:
build.sh builds libbbgpu with LTO (-flto=auto, also for sirit and FSR-Vulkan linked into it) and, when pgo/ holds a profile, with -fprofile-use (-fprofile-partial-training -fprofile-correction; functions changed since the profile compile without it). No -march: the same build runs on the Steam Deck.

Collecting a profile: BB_PGO=generate bash run.sh builds an instrumented library (-fprofile-generate -fprofile-update=atomic) that writes pgo/ every 30 s (bb:pgo thread: __gcov_dump + __gcov_reset, since the game often ends through _exit); play a few minutes of ordinary gameplay. The next plain build uses it. BB_PGO=off / BB_LTO=OFF disable them. Regenerate the profile after larger code changes.

Comparison, three runs in game (median of in-game 5 s windows, >800 draws/frame), with the new Frame stats field "GPU thread us/draw" (CPU time of the GPU command thread per draw, which tolerates small scene differences better than FPS):

build FPS GPU thread µs/draw no LTO, no PGO 73.2 7.72 LTO 74.4 7.58 (−1.8%) LTO + PGO 76.3 7.35 (−4.8%)

docs.title: Second pass: where the GPU thread's time goes, and a texture helper (2026-09-30)
docs.text:
Standing in Hunter's Nightmare, FSR 4, BB_FPS_LIMIT=0, ~85 FPS, ~1610 draws/frame.

On-CPU profile (perf, direct children): Draw 74% — BindResources 32% (textures 16%, buffers 13%), BeginRendering 8%, GetGraphicsPipeline 5%, BindVertexBuffers 4.5%, ResetBindings 4%, dynamic state 2%; DispatchDirect 6%; PM4 decode and register hashing ~9%. No function above ~5% self time: the cost is cache misses spread over the texture, buffer and barrier structures (slot_images[id], image descriptions, backing state, set writes).

Wall time (new Frame stats fields): the GPU thread is on the CPU 91% of the time and waits for guest submissions 0.5%. About 9% is blocked in Scheduler::WaitHostCopies: ~130 times per frame (EOP/EOS events, WriteData, submissions) it waits for the small guest copies queued in the recording stream, i.e. until the recording thread has recorded every command before them, plus ~4% for the copy threads (BbCopy::WaitAsync). The recording thread itself works ~40% (the rest is its spin); it is not the limit.

docs.title: Texture binding on a helper thread (opt-in: BB_TEXTURE_HELPER=1, toggle 1 << 34)
docs.text:
bb:TexBind binds a draw's textures while the GPU thread binds its buffers and resolves its vertex/index buffers (split into Resolve/Emit, toggle 1 << 35); the GPU thread joins before BeginRendering. The helper takes only the memoized path (FindImage memo valid, image clean, no scene-target proxy, no upscaler redirect, no storage images, no mip arrays, no storage buffers in the pipeline); anything else is bound after the join. The GPU thread joins before it changes image state (Runtime::BeforeImageAccess in Transit, FlushBarriers, SetBackingSamples, and in SynchronizeMemoryFromImage once a texel buffer aliases an image). 68% of draws were bound in parallel, the image was unchanged — and the frame rate too: 85.9 FPS with the helper vs 85.8 without (A/B, 6 × 16 s).

Instrumented with rdtsc: the helper's task took ~6200 cycles per fork where the same work cost ~4600 on the GPU thread, and the GPU thread still waited ~2500 cycles per fork in the join. The descriptor infos, image states and binding flags the helper writes are read by the GPU thread right after, so each draw moves them between cores; the GPU thread's own work got slower by about what it handed over. Per-draw fork/join over ~7 µs of cache-bound work does not pay on this CPU; the helper stays opt-in for other CPUs.

docs.title: Other attempts
docs.text:
change A/B kept FindView memo in the image description cache (1 << 33) + write prefetch in record chunks (1 << 32) 81.5 vs 80.8 FPS yes format check by table instead of magic_enum::enum_contains (a linear scan per texture per draw); hot Image fields (flags, binding, tracking range, backing, ticks) moved in front of ImageInfo within noise yes (no downside) host copy queue: small copies in a lock-free MPMC queue, run by the idle recording thread, the rest by the GPU thread at the wait blocked 9.5% → 4.8%, but 86.5 vs 87.2 FPS: the copying moved onto the GPU thread no no barrier tracking for read-only stream buffer ranges 85.9 vs 87.4 FPS, both phase orders (cause not found) no small host copies batched, one recorded command per 32 86.4 vs 86.2 FPS no

Fixed on the way: a draw-preparation worker could stop the process with SurfaceFormat: Unknown data_format=15 — it read a V# the guest was still writing and SurfaceFormat asserts. Workers now use TrySurfaceFormat and leave such draws to the GPU thread. It showed up with the slower PGO-instrumented build.

PGO profile regenerated for the changed code (camera rotation only, merged with the old one). Before/after, as a user builds them (37c8eac with its profile vs this state with the new one), three alternating restarts × 50 s: 86.9 vs 86.4 FPS, 6.47 vs 6.51 µs/draw — no change beyond the run-to-run spread (±1.5 FPS).

docs.title: What would scale
docs.text:
Moving work to another core per draw costs about what it saves, because the data is shared. Scaling needs splits where each thread owns its data for long stretches:

  1. Two-stage pipeline. A second thread owns the texture cache and image state (PrepareRenderState, BindTextures, BeginRendering, barriers, descriptor writes, dynamic state, draw recording) and runs a draw behind the GPU thread, which keeps decode, pipelines and the buffer cache. The second thread cannot read liverpool->regs (the GPU thread is already on later packets): it keeps its own register copy from the per-buffer deltas the draw scanner already records (AmdGpu::RegDelta). Packets that touch memory or images outside draws (DMA, WriteData, EOP/EOS, dispatches, fast clears) drain the pipeline. Estimate: the second stage takes ~30% of today's GPU thread work, less the drains. Large, delicate refactor.
  2. Less work per draw. A frame-to-frame memo of a stage's resolved textures (image ids, views, samplers) keyed by the prepared T#/S# hashes and validated by the registry generation, image cleanliness and layouts, instead of per-texture lookups.
  3. The copies before fences (~9% blocked): keep them off the GPU thread's critical path, e.g. by letting the idle draw-preparation workers drain a copy queue.

docs.title: Two-stage draw pipeline (2026-09-30)
docs.text:
vk_draw_pipe.h. The GPU command thread (stage A) keeps PM4 decoding, the register file, the constant engine and pipeline selection. A direct draw or dispatch becomes a packet in a 16 MiB ring: the 32-word register blocks written since the previous packet (Liverpool::pipe_dirty, marked by ApplyGraphicsRegisterPacket), the CB/DB size hints, each stage's user data, flattened user data and program base, and the draw parameters (for a dispatch the ComputeProgram). The draw recording thread bb:DrawRec (stage B) applies the blocks to its own register copy and runs the rest of the draw (DrawRecord, DispatchRecord): textures, buffers, render targets, barriers, descriptors, dynamic state, recording. While packets are in flight stage B owns the texture/buffer caches, the runtime, the scheduler, the scene targets, the upscaler and the motion state.

  • Stage B reads registers through Rasterizer::Regs()/CbExtent()/CsRegs() (its copy there, Liverpool's elsewhere) and shader user data through Shader::Info::UserData()/FlatUserData()/ ProgramBase(), which return the snapshot stage B installed for the stages of the current draw (Info::ud_snapshots, thread-local).
  • Everything else stage A does on stage B's state first waits for it to run dry (Rasterizer::DrainDrawPipe): every public rasterizer entry point on the GPU thread, PM4 packets other than register writes/draws/dispatches/fences (PipelinedOpcode), pending commands (ProcessCommands), compute queue packets, DumpConstRam.
  • End-of-pipe/-shader events run in order on stage B (Rasterizer::RunInOrder). A WaitRegMem on a fence value handed to stage B counts as met (Liverpool::pending_fences): stage B runs everything in stream order anyway. Unmet waits drain stage B, then yield.
  • The EOP fence is signalled by the Vulkan recording thread after the guest memory copies queued before it (Scheduler::SignalAfterHostCopies), so stage B does not wait for them.
  • A submission's prepared draws stay alive until stage B has passed them (RetireSubmission) instead of a drain at its end.
  • Faults: stage B handles its own inline, like the GPU thread (IsGpuSideThread); the GPU thread drains stage B before handling one inline. With userfaultfd, faults of the GPU thread take the locked path of guest threads.
  • DmaData to 0x3022C (skipped by the handler; ~70k/s) does not drain.
  • BB_PIPE_VERIFY=N: every Nth packet also carries the full register file and stage B reports words where its copy differs (none seen in game, menus included).
  • BB_DRAW_PIPE=0/1 overrides the default (on with 8+ hardware threads). The toggle mask is 64 bits now (bits 20-29 are raw debug toggles of the motion vectors and the upscaler, which the first measurements below also flipped): 1 << 37 whole pipeline, 1 << 38 fences on stage B, 1 << 39 WaitRegMem on pending fences, 1 << 40 dispatches, 1 << 41 fences signalled by the recording thread, 1 << 42 WriteData/DmaData/special draws/flip IRQ on stage B, 1 << 36 constant ring. Frame stats add a Draw pipe line: draws, drains that waited and why, stage A waiting, stage B busy.

Results (Hunter's Nightmare, standing, FSR 4, BB_FPS_LIMIT=0, A/B in one run):

pipeline on off 16 threads 96.1 FPS 80.6 FPS (+19%) 4 cores / 8 threads (taskset -c 0-3,8-11) 83.8 FPS 71.0 FPS (+18%)
